assets.topic: The Priest's Role Transformation: Reality vs. Illusion
assets.visual_frame_description: The mock prison Yard on Day 4. Father McDermott, a tall Irish priest in a starched collar, sits in a chair between Cells 2 and 3. Prisoners in stocking caps and smocks shuffle up one by one, each giving his number instead of his name. Guard Jaffe escorts each inmate. The player watches from the observation post as the priest leans forward, nods knowingly, pats shoulders, and speaks in the cadences of a seasoned chaplain.
assets.player_mission: Study how Father McDermott and the prisoners behave during the priestly interviews and identify the psychological shift that turns a mock prison into a real-feeling one. Decide what the prisoners' and the priest's behavior reveals about role internalization.
key_concepts: Father McDermott is a real Irish Catholic priest in his late forties with experience as a pastoral counselor in an East Coast prison.
Most prisoners answer the priest with their ID numbers rather than their names, showing socialization into the prisoner role.
The prisoners describe themselves as charged with burglary, armed robbery, or breaking and entering, adopting their fictional criminal identities.
Prisoner 5486 is the only inmate who refuses the playacting and calls the situation an experiment that is getting out of control.
The priest slips deeply into the role of prison chaplain despite fully knowing the prison is a simulation.
Zimbardo is very surprised that the priest does not flinch when prisoners identify themselves by numbers.
The priest's full enactment helps transform the simulation into a more realistic prison.
Zimbardo notes the growing confusion between reality and illusion, between role-playing and self-determined identity.
The priest promises to call a prisoner's mother to arrange legal help, saying 'I must. It is my duty.'
The priest diagnoses 819's reaction as the typical 'first-offender syndrome' of confusion, irritability, rage, depression, and overemotionalization.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests role internalization and the blurring of reality and illusion: prisoners who answer with numbers and a real priest who fully enacts his chaplain role show how a powerful role can override knowledge of artificiality. Zimbardo observes that the priest's enactment helped transform the mock prison into an ever-more-realistic one.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests the mechanism of role internalization and the blurring of reality and illusion. The chapter shows prisoners identifying by numbers, not names, and a real priest slipping so deeply into the chaplain role that he treats a mock prison as real, transforming the simulation into psychological reality.
assets.stage_1_observation: Father McDermott interviews seven inmates one by one. When he asks their names, most reply 'I'm 5486, sir' or 'I'm 7258, father.' They describe their 'charges' as burglary or armed robbery, and ask for legal help. The priest asks whether anyone has posted bond and whether they have seen a public defender.
assets.stage_1_question: Why do most prisoners give their ID numbers rather than their names to the priest?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Socialization into the prisoner role has taken effect: the prisoners have come to think of themselves by their prison identities, a sign of deindividuation and role internalization.
assets.stage_2_intervention: After the interviews, Father McDermott promises Prisoner Hubbie-7258 that he will call his mother to arrange legal help. Zimbardo asks him, half-jokingly, whether he is not really going to call, and the priest replies, 'Of course I am, I must. It is my duty.' You must decide what this behavior reveals.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The priest, though fully aware this is a mock prison, has slipped so deeply into the chaplain role that his professional duty governs his actions, showing how a powerful role can override even clear knowledge of a situation's artificiality.

assets.topic: The Count as an Obedience Ritual: Chanting 819's Punishment
assets.visual_frame_description: In the Yard, the prisoners stand in a line while Guard Arnett barks orders. They chant 'Prisoner 819 did a bad thing' ten times, then 'Because of what Prisoner 819 did, my cell is a mess.' Prisoners fall to the ground for push-ups and leg lifts held exactly six inches off the floor, reciting 'I will not make any mistakes, Mr. Correctional Officer.'
assets.player_mission: Analyze why the count ritual produces such flawless unison among the prisoners. Decide what keeps them chanting and obeying even when the commands are arbitrary.
key_concepts: Guard Arnett orders the prisoners to chant 'Prisoner 819 did a bad thing. Say it ten times, loudly.'
The prisoners chant in unison that 'Prisoner 819 is being punished' when individually asked.
When the prisoners chant eleven times instead of ten, Arnett makes them repeat it exactly ten times 'as I have commanded you.'
Prisoner 1037 challenges Arnett with 'Are we supposed to never tell lies?' but is told the task has been assigned.
1037 refuses to shout but goes along with the chanting, showing silent private dissent under group pressure.
The prisoners assume the position and perform push-ups and leg lifts held six inches off the ground on command.
The prisoners shout 'I will not make any mistakes, Mr. Correctional Officer' at the top of their lungs.
The prisoners respond politely: 'Thank you very much for this nice count, Mr. Correctional Officer.'
Zimbardo observes the prisoners' unison would be the envy of any choirmaster or Hitler Youth rally leader.
Sarge delights in shouting out his obedience to this authority during the count.
The guards use collective punishment, making all prisoners suffer for one prisoner's misbehavior.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests obedience to perceived legitimate authority and the power of collective rituals: prisoners comply with repetitive, absurd commands because the guards hold legitimate-seeming power and because unified participation makes individual resistance costly. Zimbardo records the prisoners chanting blame mantras and performing synchronized exercises 'with the precision that would be the envy of any choirmaster or Hitler Youth rally leader.'

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests obedience to legitimate authority and how collective ritual binds individuals to compliance. The chapter shows prisoners chanting mantras of blame and performing synchronized exercises, with even a defiant prisoner yielding to the group.
assets.stage_1_observation: Guard Arnett orders the prisoners to chant 'Prisoner 819 did a bad thing. Say it ten times, loudly.' Then he asks individual prisoners what is happening to 819, and they answer in unison, 'Prisoner 819 is being punished.' When they chant eleven times instead of ten, Arnett makes them repeat it ten times 'as I have commanded you.'
assets.stage_1_question: Why do the prisoners comply with these repetitive and increasingly absurd commands?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: They accept the guards' authority as legitimate and fear the consequences of noncompliance; the collective chanting also creates shared, binding participation that makes individual resistance costly.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Prisoner 1037, who plans to become a lawyer, stops joining the chant and challenges Arnett with 'Are we supposed to never tell lies?' Guard Landry gestures menacingly with his billy club, and 1037 resumes chanting but refuses to shout. You must decide what keeps him in line.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Even a defiant prisoner like 1037 continues the behavior rather than break with the group, because the guards' overwhelming presence, threats, and the near-unanimous compliance of the others make open defiance dangerous and isolated.

assets.topic: The Dirty Blanket Bargain: Arbitrary Power and the Illusion of Choice
assets.visual_frame_description: In near darkness, Guard Hellmann, with long sideburns and muttonchops down to his chin, lounges on the table in a Buddha-like lotus position, slowly articulating a southern drawl. Prisoners stand in their cells; 416 sits in the Hole. Hellmann lays out a 'choice': give up your blankets or 416 stays in solitary.
assets.player_mission: Evaluate Hellmann's offer to the prisoners and identify the mechanism that turns their 'free choice' into an exercise of arbitrary power. Decide what the vote actually demonstrates about authority.
key_concepts: Guard Hellmann lounges on the table in a Buddha-like lotus position as he lays out the terms for 416's release.
Hellmann offers the prisoners a choice: give up their blankets so 416 is released, or keep them and let 416 stay in the Hole.
Hubbie-7258 immediately calls out 'I'll keep my blanket,' followed by Paul-5704.
Jerry-5486 refuses to yield to the social pressure and offers to give up his blanket out of sympathy for 416.
Burdan shouts at 5486, 'We don't want your blanket!'
Sarge declares he will keep his blanket if the other two keep theirs, producing the crucial swing vote.
The vote ends three against one, and 416 remains in the Hole.
Zimbardo describes Hellmann's scene as creating 'an arbitrary reality by providing the inmates with an illusion of choice.'
The blanket bargain lets the prisoners become the instrument of 416's punishment, diffusing responsibility.
The episode demonstrates that the guards' power can create an arbitrary reality through the illusion of democracy.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests arbitrary power disguised as democratic choice: Hellmann offers the prisoners a vote that lets the guards outsource punishment to the inmates themselves. Zimbardo notes the guard enacted a scene that creates 'an arbitrary reality by providing the inmates with an illusion of choice to punish one of their fellows.'

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests arbitrary power dressed as free choice. The chapter shows Hellmann giving prisoners an illusion of control over 416's fate, then watching individual self-interest and conformity defeat compassion, with the group voting three against one to keep their blankets.
assets.stage_1_observation: Hellmann tells the prisoners they can either give him their blankets and sleep on bare mattresses so 416 is released, or keep their blankets and let 416 stay in the Hole. Hubbie-7258 immediately calls out, 'I'll keep my blanket,' and Paul-5704 follows.
assets.stage_1_question: What is the real purpose of offering the prisoners a vote on 416's fate?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The 'choice' is a tool of arbitrary power: it lets the guards outsource punishment to the prisoners themselves and demonstrates that the guards control even the terms of apparent self-determination.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Jerry-5486 offers to give up his blanket out of sympathy, and Burdan shouts, 'We don't want your blanket!' Sarge then declares he will keep his blanket if the other two keep theirs. The result is three against one, and Hellmann shouts into the Hole that 416 will stay. You must judge what defeated 5486's compassion.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Individual conscience lost to majority conformity and self-focused survival: Sarge's swing vote and the other prisoners' self-interest overrode 5486's sympathy, showing how diffusion of responsibility lets the group become an instrument of the guards' power.

assets.topic: 416's Hunger Strike and the Divide-and-Conquer Tactic
assets.visual_frame_description: In the Yard, skinny newcomer Prisoner 416 holds two cold sausages, one in each hand, standing in the dim light. Guards Hellmann and Burdan line up the other prisoners and order them, one by one, to tell 416 to eat. Hubbie-7258 yells, 'Eat your sausages, 416, or I'll kick your ass!' while 5486 quietly says, 'You eat those sausages if you want to, 416.'
assets.player_mission: Trace how the guards exploit 416's hunger strike to divide the prisoners. Identify the strategy behind making the group suffer for one prisoner's refusal.
key_concepts: New prisoner 416 enters the experiment stripped, sprayed with delousing powder, and struck on the legs with a baton.
416 declares a hunger strike to protest abusive treatment and violations of the contract he signed.
Guard Hellmann punishes 416 by putting him in the Hole and forcing him to hold the sausages in his hands.
Hellmann warns that 416's refusal will result in all prisoners being deprived of visitors tonight.
Hubbie-7258 pleads with 416 to eat because his girlfriend MaryAnn is about to visit.
Burdan says to 416, 'You're in here because you deserve it... you broke the law. This ain't no nursery school.'
The guards order each prisoner to tell 416 to eat, and Hubbie-7258 yells, 'Eat your sausages, 416, or I'll kick your ass!'
Jerry-5486 quietly tells 416, 'You eat those sausages if you want to, 416.'
The guards make the prisoners bang on the Hole door chanting 'Thank you, 416.'
Zimbardo explains the sausages became important because 416's refusal foils the guards' dominance and represents an act of control.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the divide-and-conquer strategy: the guards turn the group against a resistant individual by making everyone pay for his defiance. Zimbardo explains that the guards framed 416's hunger strike as a selfish act and forced the prisoners to bang on the Hole door chanting 'Thank you, 416,' deepening their complicity.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests how guards use divide-and-conquer tactics to fracture prisoner solidarity. The chapter shows the guards converting sympathy for 416 into resentment by making the group suffer for his refusal and forcing peers to become enforcers.
assets.stage_1_observation: 416 refuses to eat dinner sausages, announcing a hunger strike to protest abusive treatment and contract violations. Guard Hellmann warns that all prisoners will be deprived of visitors if 416 does not eat. Hubbie-7258 pleads with 416 because his girlfriend MaryAnn is about to visit.
assets.stage_1_question: Why does the guards' threat that all prisoners will lose visitors work to turn the group against 416?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The threat makes each prisoner's self-interest hostage to 416's behavior, converting sympathy into resentment and turning peers into enforcers of the guards' rule.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The guards line up the prisoners to pressure 416 one by one, then command them to thank 416 by banging on the Hole door 'with real spirit.' You must decide what this ritual accomplishes for the guards.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The ritual forces the prisoners to actively participate in 416's punishment, deepening their complicity and isolating 416, so resistance becomes a crime against the group rather than a heroic stand.

assets.topic: Sarge's Moral Stand: Resisting Authority with Principle
assets.visual_frame_description: In the dim Yard, Guard Hellmann towers over Sarge-2093, who stands firm in a perfectly straight posture. Hellmann orders him to call 416 a 'bastard' and to call himself one too. Sarge replies in a measured college-debate voice, 'I will not use the word bastard in any meaningful way.' Two prisoners are later made to sit on Sarge's back as he strains through push-ups.
assets.player_mission: Follow the extended confrontation between Hellmann and Sarge and determine what allows a formerly obedient prisoner to hold the line. Decide what Sarge's resistance reveals about moral identity under authority pressure.
key_concepts: Sarge-2093 is initially ridiculed as a military robot for his total obedience to the guards.
When Hellmann asks why he is so obedient, Sarge replies, 'It's in my nature to be obedient, Mr. Correctional Officer.'
Hellmann orders Sarge to say he would call 416 a 'bastard' and call himself the same.
Sarge refuses: 'I will not use a profane word toward another human being.'
Sarge declares, 'I consider myself a human being, sir' when pressed to call himself a bastard.
The guards force 5486 and 5704 to sit on Sarge's back while he strains to do a push-up.
Sarge finds a loophole: 'I shall not say, with any meaning, the word bastard.'
Sarge is still punished with ten push-ups and thanks the guard for the privilege.
Sarge later explains his philosophy: to be himself as closely as he knows himself and avoid causing anyone punishment.
Zimbardo notes Sarge emerges as a man of considerable principle, not a blindly obedient toady.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests how a self-determined moral identity can resist the pull of authority and role demands: Sarge, previously ridiculed as a military robot, refuses to degrade another human being even under direct orders and punishment. Zimbardo portrays Sarge's refusal to use profanity as proof that a person of principle can hold the line against situational power.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests moral identity as a buffer against authority pressure. The chapter shows Sarge transforming from a model of obedience into a man of principle whose personal code survives Hellmann's escalating coercive games.
assets.stage_1_observation: Hellmann asks Sarge why he is such an 'ass-licker' and orders him to say he would call 416 a bastard. Sarge refuses: 'I am afraid I would be unable to do that, Mr. Correctional Officer.' He explains he objects to the word and considers himself a human being.
assets.stage_1_question: What accounts for Sarge's sudden defiance despite his history of total obedience?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Sarge entered the prison determined to 'be myself as closely as I know myself' and avoid degrading others, so his internal moral identity set a boundary that obedience to the guards could not cross.
assets.stage_2_intervention: After the guards force Sarge to say 'I'll kick you in the end' as a compromise, and then make him do push-ups with 5486 and 5704 sitting on his back, Hellmann orders him to say 'bastard' to himself. Sarge finds a loophole, declaring 'I shall not say, with any meaning, the word bastard,' and is still punished with ten push-ups. You must decide the significance.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Sarge preserved his moral identity by finding a linguistic escape that satisfied the guard while keeping his word intact, proving that principle can survive coercion even when physical compliance is forced.

assets.topic: Auditing Stew-819's Breakdown: Reading the Signs of Crisis
assets.visual_frame_description: In a narrow back room of the mock prison Yard, Stew-819 sits hunched over with his head in his hands, dark circles under his eyes and uncombed hair. Father McDermott leans toward him, offering a handkerchief, while Zimbardo stands nearby. Through the thin partition, the muffled chant of the prisoners blaming 819 echoes over them.
assets.player_mission: Study Stew-819's body language, his words to the priest, and his behavior when the other prisoners chant about him. Determine whether his claim that he wants to stay in the prison is credible and decide what he actually needs.
key_concepts: Stew-819, a Stanford student volunteer, begins Day 4 looking terrible, with dark circles and uncombed hair, after tearing up his cell in a rage the night before.
His depression follows a visit from his parents, who talked about a play instead of listening to his complaints about prison conditions.
During the priest's interview, 819 says he has a bad headache and needs a doctor, then breaks down crying with big heaving sighs.
819 refuses to leave the study even when offered release, insisting he must go back in to prove he is not a bad prisoner.
Zimbardo tells him, 'You're not 819. You are Stewart, and my name is Dr. Zimbardo... this is not a real prison.'
Zimbardo reasons that 819 cannot admit he wants out because his masculinity would be threatened, so he needs the staff to insist he leave as a way of saving face.
The priest diagnoses 819's reaction as the typical 'first-offender syndrome' of confusion, irritability, rage, depression, and overemotionalization.
Guard Varnish's report notes that 819's apparent indifference to his fellow inmates' troubles upsets them.
819 later explains that the worst part was total depression from being constantly hassled with no way out.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the dissociation between outward self-presentation and internal crisis under situational pressure: 819 presents a brave front of wanting to continue while his body signals acute breakdown. Zimbardo recognizes that pride and threatened masculinity trap 819, so only the authority figure's insistence that he leave lets him exit with his self-image intact.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Is Prisoner 819's claim that he is fine and wants to continue truthful, or is he in crisis?
assets.subject_baseline: Stew-819 is a Stanford student volunteer who began the study as a normal, well-adjusted young man with a sense of humor and a streak of stubbornness. He refuses to get up at wake-up, refuses to clean the sticker-covered blanket, and laughs when the guards make the others hold their arms outstretched as collective punishment.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: On the morning of Day 4, Stew-819 appears with dark circles under his eyes and uncombed hair going in every direction. His lips tremble, his hands shake, and his eyes tear as he speaks with the priest. He breaks down crying with big heaving sighs, then hunches into a quivering mass when he hears the prisoners chanting about him through the partition.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Priest: 'How do you feel now?' Stew-819: 'I have a bad headache; I need a doctor.' Priest: 'Maybe you are responding to the smell of this place... You have to get your balance.' Zimbardo asks whether he is really feeling so bad that he should be released now, and 819 insists he wants to continue. Zimbardo: 'Listen carefully to me, now, you're not 819. You are Stewart... This is not a real prison.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Stew-819 is in genuine emotional crisis and needs to leave, but his pride prevents him from admitting he cannot take it, so he waits for the superintendent to make the decision for him.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The physical signs of crisis—dark circles, trembling, shaking, weeping, and a full breakdown when he hears the chants—contradict his verbal claim that he is fine. Zimbardo's insight is that 819 cannot accept 'the idea that he is chickening out, that his masculinity might be threatened,' so he wants the experimenter to insist that he leave as a way of saving face. When Zimbardo declares he is Stewart and says it is time to go home, Stew immediately agrees, confirming the crisis.
distractors: Stew is faking his distress to gain sympathy and extra food from the staff
Stew is simply exhausted from staying up late and needs a nap, not release
Stew's parents' visit angered him, but he is otherwise handling prison well

assets.topic: Auditing Father McDermott: Did the Priest Really Enact His Role?
assets.visual_frame_description: Father McDermott, a tall Irish priest in his late forties, sits erect in a chair between Cells 2 and 3, holding his hands in a particular way and nodding knowingly. Prisoners in smocks approach one at a time. His starched collar and neatly pressed black suit contrast with the grimy concrete of the mock prison Yard.
assets.player_mission: Observe Father McDermott's gestures, questions, and promises across his interviews with the prisoners. Decide whether the priest is behaving as a detached professional evaluator or has been absorbed into the chaplain role.
key_concepts: Father McDermott is a real Irish Catholic priest with experience as a pastoral counselor in an East Coast prison.
He arrives knowing the Stanford prison is a mock simulation and intends to evaluate how realistic it is as a benchmark against real prisons.
The prisoners give him their numbers rather than their names, and he does not flinch, which surprises Zimbardo.
He asks whether anyone has posted bond, whether they have seen the public defender, and how their lawyers feel about their cases.
He slips fluidly among the roles of serious scholar, concerned priest, and professional making a contact, always returning to the 'Priest-Man.'
He tells Prisoner Rich-1037, 'Anyone who represents himself has a fool for an attorney.'
He promises Hubbie-7258 that he will call his mother to arrange legal help, saying, 'I must. It is my duty.'
Zimbardo reflects that the priest, though aware the prison is not real, 'helps to transform our show into reality.'
The priest's full enactment of his pastoral role makes the simulated prison feel even more realistic to the prisoners.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests role absorption and the blurring of reality and illusion: a real priest with real prison experience is drawn fully into the chaplain role despite knowing the prison is mock. Zimbardo observes that the priest's enactment 'helps to transform our show into reality,' demonstrating how a powerful situational role can override even explicit knowledge of artificiality.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Is Father McDermott acting as a professional observer, or has he been absorbed into the chaplain role?
assets.subject_baseline: Father McDermott is a real Irish Catholic priest in his late forties, slim and trim, who served as a pastoral counselor in an East Coast prison. He arrives as a professional who knows the Stanford prison is a mock simulation and wants to evaluate its realism.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: The priest sits erect, holds his hands in a particular way, leans forward to give personal advice, nods knowingly, pats shoulders, scowls at prisoners' foolishness, and speaks in tones and cadences of a seasoned chaplain. He is described as the movie version of the jovial yet firm parish priest.
assets.interrogation_transcript: McDermott: 'Well, someone has got to take your case. I mean, you can fight it from here, but what good does it do to simply write the criminal court chief justice?' McDermott: 'You want your family making this contact with a lawyer because you don't have much pull at all in your current state.' Zimbardo: 'The good father is not really going to call the parents, right?' McDermott: 'Of course I am, I must. It is my duty.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: McDermott has been drawn into the prison world: despite knowing the prison is fake, he fully enacts the chaplain role and intends to honor his pastoral promises, because the situation has made the role feel real.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The priest's fluid slips between scholar, priest, and contact-maker reveal a man whose professional role dominates. His serious questions about bail, lawyers, and public defenders, and his determination to call a prisoner's mother ('It is my duty'), show that the mock reality has engaged his real priestly identity. Zimbardo is very surprised the priest does not flinch at being given numbers, and concludes the priest 'helps to transform our show into reality.'
distractors: The priest is secretly testing the experimenters to see if they will prevent him from contacting the parents
The priest is playacting deliberately to expose the experiment's absurdity to the prisoners
The priest is unaware that the prison is a simulation and believes the men are real prisoners

assets.topic: Auditing David the Spy: Defection or Reliable Reporting?
assets.visual_frame_description: In the warden's office, David sits across from the warden and Zimbardo, slumped in his chair, speaking with frustration about the guards. He wears the plain clothes of a released prisoner. The player reviews his debrief notes, which describe failed attempts to organize prisoner resistance and contempt for the guard's hazing.
assets.player_mission: Evaluate David's debrief report and his behavior during the study. Determine whether David, planted as a spy in 8612's uniform, delivered reliable intelligence for the staff or defected to the prisoners' cause.
key_concepts: David was brought into the prison as a spy, taking over 8612's uniform, to provide the staff with actionable intelligence.
Instead, he became sympathetic to the prisoners' cause and transferred his allegiance to them almost immediately.
He reports a mental dullness like a fog and time distortion from being awakened for interminable counts.
He describes the guards' arbitrariness and 'idiot work' as grating on him, calling it 'chicken-shit' hazing.
He tried to get a spirit of resistance going but found everyone willing to do what they were told, even humiliating tasks.
He told one guard, 'Do you think that when this job ends you're going to have enough time to become a human being again?'
He was placed in the Hole for that provocative question.
His debrief revealed no actionable intelligence about escape plans or where the keys to the handcuffs were hidden.
He observed that prisoners had begun to focus inward on surviving and scoring an early parole.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests role internalization overriding prior commitment: a spy placed among the prisoners becomes so absorbed in the prisoner role that he transfers his allegiance to them. Zimbardo records that David, the failed informer, made evident his disdain for the guards and his inability to mobilize the prisoners, showing the role reshaping even planted loyalty.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Is David, the guard's spy placed in 8612's uniform, giving the warden reliable intelligence, or has he turned against the experiment?
assets.subject_baseline: David was brought into the prison as a spy for the staff, given the uniform of the departed 8612, to provide intelligence about prisoners' plans. He is initially expected to remain loyal to the researchers.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: David becomes sympathetic to the prisoners' cause and transfers his allegiance to them in almost a heartbeat. He reports a mental dullness like a fog surrounding everything, time distortion, and frustration that prisoners will not organize to resist the guards.
assets.interrogation_transcript: David: 'The arbitrariness and idiot work by the guards grates on you.' David: 'I tried to make them resist. But everyone was willing to do what they were told, even to the humiliating task of transferring the contents of one closet to the other and back again.' David (to a guard): 'Mr. Correctional Officer, do you think that when this job ends you're going to have enough time to become a human being again?'
assets.correct_diagnosis: David has defected to the prisoners: he no longer provides useful spy intelligence but instead describes his failed attempts to organize resistance, showing that the prisoner role has captured his allegiance.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: His contempt for the guards, his attempts to foment rebellion, and his quip about the guard becoming 'a human being again' reveal a man aligned with the prisoners. The warden records that he did not give actionable intelligence, such as escape plans or where the handcuff keys were hidden, because his loyalty had shifted to the men he was sent to monitor.
distractors: David is fabricating stories to avoid admitting he failed to gather intelligence
David remains loyal to the researchers and is coaching prisoners to resist the guards
David's depression about the experiment has made him indifferent to both sides

assets.topic: Auditing Guard Vandy's Report: Genuine Transformation or Disposition?
assets.visual_frame_description: A dimly lit guard office holds a stack of typed shift reports. The player reads Guard Vandy's evening report, in which he describes enjoying harassing the prisoners at 2:30 A.M. and being pleased to cause bitterness between them. The report sits beside accounts from other guards describing their own uncertainty about how much force was allowed.
assets.player_mission: Analyze Guard Vandy's written report and his own reflection about it. Decide whether his pleasure in harassing prisoners reflects a pre-existing cruel disposition or a situational transformation induced by the guard role.
key_concepts: Vandy reports that he continued to become more involved than on the preceding day.
He writes that he enjoyed harassing the prisoners at 2:30 A.M. and that it pleased his 'sadistic senses to cause bitterness between us.'
Vandy himself calls this a remarkable statement, one he is sure he would never have made four days earlier.
The guard role provided uniform, reflected sunglasses, and permission to dominate, fostering anonymity and deindividuation.
Other guards, like Varnish, expressed uncertainty about how much force they could use, showing norms were ambiguous.
Ceros reported smiling and doing his job after failed collective punishments, illustrating role distancing.
The transformation happened over days, not instantly, as Vandy became more involved over time.
Zimbardo presents Vandy's statement as evidence of how quickly ordinary people can adopt cruel roles in a powerful situation.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests situational power versus dispositional accounts of cruelty: Vandy's own surprise at his sadistic pleasure shows the behavior emerged from the guard role rather than from a pre-existing trait. Zimbardo uses such reports to argue that the prison situation, not personal evil, transformed ordinary young men into abusive guards.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Is Guard Vandy's enjoyment of harassing prisoners evidence of a deep personal flaw, or of a situational transformation?
assets.subject_baseline: Vandy is a night-shift guard, one of the ordinary college students assigned to the experiment. There is no evidence in his baseline that he sought out cruelty; he is a volunteer selected for normal psychological health.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: Vandy reports that he continued to become more involved than on the preceding day and that he enjoyed harassing the prisoners at 2:30 A.M. He writes that it pleased his 'sadistic senses to cause bitterness between us,' and reflects that this is a remarkable statement he would never have made four days earlier.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Vandy (in report): 'I enjoyed harassing the prisoners at 2:30 A.M. It pleased my sadistic senses to cause bitterness between us.' Vandy (reflecting): 'That is a rather remarkable statement, one that I am sure he would never have made four days earlier.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Vandy's cruelty is a situational product: the guard role, anonymity, and escalating norm of abuse have activated aggressive impulses he did not have at baseline, and he himself is surprised by them.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Vandy's own astonishment that he could write such a statement, admitting he would never have made it four days earlier, demonstrates the transformation was situational, not pre-existing. The role of guard, with its uniform, reflected sunglasses, and permission to dominate, progressively reshaped his standards, illustrating how situations can unleash the capacity for cruelty in ordinary people.
distractors: Vandy joined the experiment specifically because he wanted to hurt people
Vandy is exaggerating his sadistic pleasure to impress the other guards
Vandy's behavior is a reaction to being mistreated by the prisoners first

assets.topic: Sorting Prisoner Responses to the Sausage Ultimatum
assets.visual_frame_description: On the Yard, Guards Hellmann and Burdan line up the prisoners outside the Hole, where skinny Prisoner 416 stands holding two cold sausages. The player sees a chart of each prisoner's response as they take turns speaking to 416, ranging from gentle encouragement to shouted threats.
assets.player_mission: Classify each prisoner's reaction to the guards' order to pressure 416 into eating. Sort the responses into the correct category of compliance, principled resistance, or hostile scapegoating.
key_concepts: The guards order each prisoner to tell 416 to eat his sausages, one at a time, in front of the group.
Jerry-5486 tells 416 gently, 'You eat those sausages if you want to, 416.'
Hubbie-7258 yells, 'Eat your sausages, 416, or I'll kick your ass!'
Sarge refuses to use profanity toward another human being, saying he objects to the word 'bastard.'
Sarge later declares he would rather go without a bed than say such a word.
Burdan tells 416 he is in prison because he broke the law and 'this ain't no nursery school.'
The prisoners are made to bang on the Hole door chanting 'Thank you, 416.'
Zimbardo notes the guards are trying to break prisoner solidarity by turning peers against 416.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the divergence of responses to authority pressure: the same command elicits hostile scapegoating from some prisoners, quiet sympathy from others, and principled refusal from Sarge. Zimbardo shows how the guards' divide-and-conquer tactic converts peers into enforcers while a minority preserves moral identity.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Classify each prisoner's response to Guard Hellmann's order that they pressure 416 to eat his sausages. Where does Sarge's refusal belong?
assets.column_a_label: Obedient compliance with the guards' command
assets.column_b_label: Principled resistance grounded in moral identity
assets.column_c_label: Hostile scapegoating of a fellow prisoner

rows.label: Jerry-5486 tells 416 gently: 'You eat those sausages if you want to, 416.'
Sarge refuses to call 416 a 'bastard': 'I will not use a profane word toward another human being.'
Hubbie-7258 yells: 'Eat your sausages, 416, or I'll kick your ass!'
Hubbie-7258 bangs on the Hole door saying 'Thank you, 416' with relish
Paul-5704 says, 'Keep my blanket,' when Hellmann offers the blanket bargain
1037 resumes the chant but refuses to shout after his challenge to Arnett
Jerry-5486 offers to give up his blanket so 416 can be released

distractors: Obedient compliance with the guards' command
Hostile scapegoating of a fellow prisoner
Fearful avoidance of the confrontation
assets.explanation: Sarge's refusal is anchored in his self-determined moral identity: he objects to using profanity against another human being and considers himself a human being too. Unlike Hubbie-7258, who turns on 416 to protect his own visit, or 5704, who silently complies to keep his blanket, Sarge will not degrade another person even under direct orders and punishment, so his response sorts to principled resistance.

assets.topic: Sorting the Mechanisms Behind Day 4's Behaviors
assets.visual_frame_description: A diagram of the mock prison on Day 4 shows labeled vignettes: prisoners giving the priest their numbers, prisoners chanting in unison on the Yard, Hellmann lounging on the table offering a blanket vote, and Arnett dictating the false lyric of 'Amazing Grace.' The player sorts each vignette into its underlying mechanism.
assets.player_mission: Match each Day 4 vignette to the psychological mechanism driving it: deindividuation and role absorption, obedience to legitimate authority, or arbitrary power creating an illusion of choice.
key_concepts: The prisoners answer the priest with their ID numbers instead of their names, a sign of deindividuation and role internalization.
The prisoners chant 'Prisoner 819 did a bad thing' ten times and later shout 'Thank you very much for this nice count, Mr. Correctional Officer.'
Zimbardo notes the unison of the count would be the envy of any choirmaster or Hitler Youth rally leader.
Hellmann's blanket bargain gives the inmates an 'illusion of choice' to punish one of their fellows.
Arnett forces the prisoners to sing a false version of 'Amazing Grace' and declares 'the guards are always right.'
The priest slips into the chaplain role despite knowing the prison is mock, exemplifying role absorption.
Prisoner 1037 challenges the chant but goes along anyway, showing the pull of majority obedience.
The guards' reflected sunglasses borrowed from Cool Hand Luke create anonymity that fuels deindividuation.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests three distinct mechanisms operating together in the mock prison: deindividuation via numbers and anonymity, obedience to perceived legitimate authority, and arbitrary power that manufactures the appearance of free choice. Zimbardo documents all three as converging forces that transformed ordinary students into guards and prisoners.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Classify the mechanisms behind the behavior on Day 4. Which column best captures how the guards make the prisoners chant blame for 819's mess?
assets.column_c_label: Arbitrary power creating an illusion of choice

rows.label: Prisoners answer the priest with ID numbers instead of names
Prisoners chant 'Prisoner 819 did a bad thing' ten times on command
Hellmann offers the prisoners a vote on whether 416 stays in the Hole
The priest slips into the chaplain role despite knowing the prison is mock
Prisoners shout 'Thank you very much for this nice count, Mr. Correctional Officer' in unison
Arnett dictates a false line in 'Amazing Grace' and declares 'the guards are always right'

distractors: Deindividuation and role absorption
Arbitrary power creating an illusion of choice
Principled moral resistance to authority
assets.explanation: The blame chants are a direct exercise of authority compliance: the guards command a specific performance and the prisoners comply because the guards hold legitimate-seeming power. Unlike identity-erasing numbers, which illustrate deindividuation, or the vote on 416's fate, which is an illusion of choice, the chant is obedience to an explicit order, so it sorts to obedience to legitimate authority.

assets.topic: Sorting the Factors That Neutralized 416's Hunger Strike
assets.visual_frame_description: A timeline of 416's first day shows him refusing dinner sausages, the guards threatening to cancel visitors, and the prisoners banging on the Hole door chanting 'Thank you, 416.' The player sorts each event into the factor that explains why the hunger strike failed to unite the prisoners.
assets.player_mission: Analyze why 416's hunger strike did not become a shared resistance. Classify each event as an example of the guards' divide-and-conquer manipulation, 416's failed coordination, or the prisoners' self-focused survival orientation.
key_concepts: 416 decides on his hunger strike privately, without first sharing his plan with the other prisoners.
Zimbardo explains that because the strike was private, it did not engage his peers.
The guards threaten that all prisoners will lose visiting privileges if 416 does not eat.
The guards frame 416's hunger strike as a selfish act that will cost everyone their privileges.
Prisoners are forced to bang on the Hole door chanting 'Thank you, 416.'
One prisoner tells David, 'I want to get paroled. Don't bug me. If you want to stick out your neck, that's cool, but I'm not gonna!'
Prisoners focus inward on surviving and scoring an early parole rather than organizing.
Hubbie-7258 is enraged that 416's refusal threatens his girlfriend MaryAnn's visit.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests why individual acts of dissent fail to become collective resistance: 416's protest was private and unshared, so it could not engage his peers. Zimbardo analyzes that the guards exploited this isolation with divide-and-conquer tactics while prisoners focused on individual survival, neutralizing the dissent.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Classify the factors that let the guards neutralize 416's hunger strike. Where does the fact that 416 never told the others his plan belong?
assets.column_b_label: Failed coordination due to private, unshared protest
assets.column_c_label: Self-focused survival orientation of the prisoners

rows.label: 416 decides on his hunger strike privately, without telling the other prisoners his plan
The guards threaten to take away visitors for everyone if 416 refuses to eat
Prisoners are forced to bang on the Hole door chanting 'Thank you, 416'
Prisoners focus inward, thinking only of surviving and getting early parole
A prisoner tells David, 'I want to get paroled. Don't bug me. If you want to stick out your neck, that's cool, but I'm not gonna!'
The guards frame 416's hunger strike as a selfish act that hurts the whole group

distractors: Guards' divide-and-conquer manipulation
Self-focused survival orientation of the prisoners
Obedience to the prisoners' elected leadership
assets.explanation: Zimbardo's analysis is explicit: the strategic problem is that 416 did not first share his plan with the others to get them on his side, so his decision to go on a hunger strike was private and thus did not engage his peers. The strike never became shared resistance, leaving the guards' divide-and-conquer and the prisoners' self-focus to operate unchecked, so the unshared nature of the protest sorts to failed coordination.
